Who records deeds in Jefferson County, Colorado?

The Jefferson County Clerk and Recorder records deeds, deeds of trust and other land documents for the county. The Recording Division sits in the Administration and Courts building at 100 Jefferson County Parkway, Suite 2560, Golden, CO 80419, and the office phone is 303-271-8168.

Counter hours are Monday to Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the third Thursday of each month opening at 8 a.m. The county's recording page does not list Friday hours, so plan to submit a deed earlier in the week or send it by mail or an approved e-recording vendor. You can also book a visit online through the county recording page.

Once a document is recorded it becomes part of the public record and the county archives. That is the step that puts a buyer's name on the title in the eyes of everyone who searches later.

Where is Jefferson County and what is in it?

Jefferson County sits along the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains, next to Denver, and its county seat is Golden. Lakewood is the largest city. The county covers about 774 square miles and runs roughly 54 miles from end to end.

Incorporated places include Arvada (part), Edgewater, Golden, Lakewood, Littleton (part), Westminster (part), Wheat Ridge, Bow Mar (part), Lakeside, Morrison, Mountain View and Superior (part). Conifer, Pine and Pine Junction are unincorporated mountain communities. Ten counties touch Jefferson County, including Boulder, Denver, Douglas and Clear Creek.

Jefferson County was one of the territory's original 17 counties, reorganized on November 1, 1861. Gold found along the South Platte River in 1858 started the Pike's Peak Gold Rush, and Golden was founded in 1859. Today the Coors brewery in Golden, the Colorado School of Mines and the Denver Federal Center in Lakewood anchor the local job base.

Because the county mixes city blocks with canyon and foothill lots, a deed here can land in a municipal building department or an unincorporated one. That matters later in this guide, when we get to wildfire rules.

What does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson County?

Most letter or legal size documents carry a flat recording fee of $43 per document, no matter how many pages. A state documentary fee applies on top for transfer deeds with consideration above $500.

ItemAmount listed by the county or statute
Standard document up to 8.5 x 14 inches$43 flat fee per document
Plats and documents larger than 8.5 x 14 inches$40 per document
Documentary fee on a deed$0.10 per $1,000 of consideration when it exceeds $500
Digital copiesFree
Certification of a copy$1 per document
Documents tied to a death recordFree

The documentary fee comes from C.R.S. 39-13-102, which sets it at one cent per $100 of consideration. As a plain illustration, a $600,000 sale works out to $60. The fee falls on the person who submits the deed for recording, and the clerk collects it.

The county's separate fee page shows an older looking schedule with different per page numbers, so rely on the recording page and ask the office to confirm the total before you mail a check.

How do you submit a deed for recording?

You can bring a standard size deed to the counter, mail it, or use an approved e-recording vendor. Large format documents cannot be taken in person and must go through an approved vendor.

  • In person: standard size documents only, at the Golden office during counter hours.
  • By mail: include the document, correct payment, a return mailing address and a phone number.
  • E-recording: required for large format items; plats can be recorded electronically only through the county's contracted third party vendor.

Mail is the slowest route. The county says returned documents take 2 to 4 weeks, and it refunds only overpayments of $10 or more, so a short check can hold up the whole filing. Escrow and title companies usually handle this step for a sale, but when a deed moves outside a formal closing, the sender carries the risk.

What must a Jefferson County deed include?

The recorder requires the grantee's address on the document, per statute. Clerks cannot tell you which legal form to use, so the deed should be drafted and checked before it reaches the counter.

Consideration also matters. Under the documentary fee statute, property is treated as residential unless the instrument clearly says otherwise, and a deed that states no consideration or $500 or less can still be measured against the sales price on a related declaration. A deed that understates the price therefore does not make the fee go away.

  • Names of the grantor and grantee as they appear on the prior deed.
  • A legal description, not just a street address.
  • The grantee's mailing address.
  • A statement of consideration, so the fee is figured on the right number.

How does the Public Trustee fit in when a loan is paid off?

The Jefferson County Public Trustee handles foreclosures of deeds of trust and the release of deeds of trust that were recorded through its office. It sits at Suite 2510 of the same building, phone 303-271-8580. The county notes that Public Trustee fees rose under HB 25-1269 on July 1, 2025.

Releases for private trustee mortgage transactions are directed to the Clerk and Recorder instead, at 303-271-8121. A seller whose old lien never got released can find that a buyer's lender or title company refuses to move forward, so it is worth checking the record early.

The Public Trustee does not run judicial foreclosures, which belong to the Sheriff, and foreclosure records stay public even after a default is cured or a foreclosure is withdrawn.

How can owners guard against recording fraud?

Jefferson County offers a free Recording Notification Service that sends alerts when a document is recorded in your name. Owners who sign up can spot a forged deed or a lien they did not authorize.

The office also warns that it will never ask for payment by wire transfer. If an unexpected email or call asks for money for a recording, treat it as a scam and phone the office at a number from the county site.

What do sellers in unincorporated Jefferson County need to know about wildfire rules?

Homes in the unincorporated wildland urban interface now fall under the Jefferson County Wildfire Resiliency Code, approved March 10, 2026 and effective July 1, 2026. It is not retroactive, so it applies to new construction and exterior alterations such as additions, deck replacements, re-siding and re-roofing.

A roof replacement covering 25% or more of the roof must be a Class A assembly, and siding replacement of 25% or more must use allowed materials. Smaller repairs, interior work and painting are exempt. The county's defensible space page describes three zones out to 100 feet from a structure.

For a seller in Conifer, Pine or the canyons, that means a roof or deck project before listing can trigger permit steps. Selling the house as is, without starting that work, avoids it. County staff say no grants are offered, though the SLASH program takes defensible space debris at reduced cost.

What do Jefferson County sellers usually face before closing?

Most sellers deal with three offices besides the recorder: the Assessor for value, the Treasurer for taxes and the Public Trustee for liens. Each has its own deadline.

  • Assessor: real property appeals run May 1 through June 8 each year.
  • Treasurer: taxes are paid in arrears, so 2025 taxes were payable in 2026, and the notice goes out in late January.
  • Public Trustee: any recorded deed of trust needs a release before the title is clean.
  • Recorder: the new deed has to be submitted with the right fee and a grantee address.

If a house has deferred repairs, an inherited title or a stack of back taxes, a cash sale to a direct buyer can skip showings and lender conditions, but the recording steps above still apply to every sale in Jefferson County. You can read the county's tax pieces in our Jefferson County property tax guide.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson County, Colorado?

The county lists a flat $43 per standard size document, plus a state documentary fee of $0.10 per $1,000 of consideration on deeds above $500. Large plats and oversize documents are $40 each. Confirm the exact total with the Clerk and Recorder before mailing payment.

Does Jefferson County, CO charge a transfer tax?

Colorado's statute imposes a documentary fee of one cent per $100 of consideration, paid by whoever submits the deed.

How long does it take to get a recorded deed back by mail?

The county says returned documents take 2 to 4 weeks by mail. Overpayments of $10 or more are refunded, but a payment that is too low can delay the filing.

Can I record a deed in person on a Friday?

The county's recording page lists Monday to Thursday hours of 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and does not list Friday hours, so call 303-271-8168 first or use mail or e-recording.

Who releases an old deed of trust in Jefferson County?

Releases of deeds of trust handled through the Public Trustee go through that office at 303-271-8580. The county directs releases for private trustee mortgage transactions to the Clerk and Recorder at 303-271-8121.

What does the Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder do when a house sells?

The Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder is the office that records deeds and mortgages for property in the county. Recording puts the new owner's name in the public record, and in Colorado it is also the moment the documentary fee is collected. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102, anyone who offers a deed or other title-conveying instrument for recording pays that fee to the county clerk and recorder, in addition to the ordinary recording charges.

The office is not the same as the treasurer or the assessor. It does not bill property tax or set values. Its role in a sale is narrower: take the signed deed, check that it can be recorded, collect the fee and make the document part of the public record.

Call the office or check its site before you send anything for recording, and ask what form of payment it takes.

What is the Colorado documentary fee, and how much is it?

The documentary fee is one cent for each $100 of consideration, counting any major fraction of $100 as a full unit. No fee is due if the total consideration is $500 or less. For most house sales, that works out to ten cents for every $1,000 of price.

Sale priceDocumentary fee at one cent per $100
$250,000$25.00
$400,000$40.00
$600,000$60.00
$900,000$90.00

These amounts come from applying the statutory rate to round prices. They are examples, not quotes. The statute also counts liens and encumbrances and required charges as consideration, so the base can be larger than the price on the contract.

For property in more than one county in the same deal, each county collects its own share based on the consideration attributable to the parcels there. The person recording the instrument allocates the total among the counties.

How does Colorado decide whether a sale is residential?

Colorado treats a property as residential unless the deed carries a conspicuous statement that the property is not to be regarded as residential. That statement has to be on the instrument when it is signed. It cannot be added afterward.

  • Residential: consideration is the amount on the conveyance document. If that is missing or $500 or less and a declaration was filed under section 39-14-102, the total sales price on the declaration is used.
  • Commercial or industrial: the full sales price is treated as paid for the real property, unless separate consideration for personal property appears on the use tax return or declaration.
  • Supporting evidence is not recorded or made public. The clerk passes it to the county assessor, who keeps it confidential.

That confidentiality rule is why a recorded deed can show a fee but not every detail of the price. It also means the assessor can see what the property sold for even when the deed stays quiet.

Which recorder handles my house if it is in Aurora, Glendale or Centennial?

The county in which the parcel sits decides the recorder. Aurora spreads across Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties. Of its 386,261 residents in 2020, 336,035 lived in Arapahoe County, so most Aurora homes are recorded in Arapahoe, but a house in the Adams or Douglas parts is not.

Glendale is an exclave of Arapahoe County entirely surrounded by Denver, so its deeds still go to Arapahoe County even though Denver is next door. Centennial, formed in 2001 from unincorporated Arapahoe County, is listed as an Arapahoe County city.

CityCounty recording office
Littleton (county seat)Arapahoe County
CentennialArapahoe County
EnglewoodArapahoe County
Glendale (surrounded by Denver)Arapahoe County
Aurora, Arapahoe portionArapahoe County
Aurora, Adams or Douglas portionAdams or Douglas County

How do county boundaries and history affect an old Arapahoe County deed?

Arapahoe County was one of Colorado's original 17 counties, organized in 1861, and it once covered a far larger area. Adams County was created from part of it in 1901, though Wikipedia notes the formal start was delayed until November 15, 1902. A deed for land that is now in Adams County may carry old Arapahoe County references in its history.

That matters when a seller is working from an inherited paper file. Check the current county for the parcel rather than relying on the county named in an older document.

Cities have shifted too. Centennial did not exist before 2001, and Aurora was platted as Fletcher in 1891 and became Aurora in 1928. Confirm the county from the parcel record, not from the city on a mailing address.

What should a seller check before a deed is recorded?

Look at the consideration, the classification and the county. Each can change the fee or send the document to the wrong office.

  • The price stated on the deed, and whether liens or required charges are counted in it.
  • Whether the deed says the property is not residential. If it says nothing, Colorado treats it as residential.
  • Which county the parcel sits in, especially for Aurora.
  • Whether more than one county is involved, in which case the person recording splits the consideration.
  • A copy of the recorded deed once it comes back, for your records.

The signed document cannot be amended later to add the non-residential statement, so raise any question about classification before signing. Your title or escrow company can usually tell you how it handles the fee at closing.

What is selling a house like in Arapahoe County?

Arapahoe County mixes some of the densest suburbs on the Front Range with open plains, so no two sellers face the same situation. The county is 72 miles long and only a few miles wide in places. Strasburg, Deer Trail and Byers on the east side have their own school districts, while the west side is split between Littleton, Englewood, Sheridan and Cherry Creek.

The employer base shapes the market. Buckley Space Force Base, the Anschutz Medical Campus and Children's Hospital Colorado draw staff to Aurora. Comcast, Arrow Electronics and United Launch Alliance anchor Centennial. People relocating for jobs, or families settling an estate, often prefer a clean closing date to a long listing.

Cherry Creek State Park on the southwest edge of Aurora, where Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass in 1993, shows how much open land sits inside the metro area. Homes near parks, rail stops and the airport corridor can look quite different on paper from homes farther east.

  • Confirm the county before you pick a recorder or treasurer.
  • Ask the title company for the recording instructions it will follow.
  • Plan for the documentary fee on top of recording charges.
  • Keep the closing statement, since the assessor receives sale details from the clerk.

Frequently asked questions

What is the documentary fee in Colorado?

One cent per $100 of consideration, or ten cents per $1,000. Nothing is owed on $500 or less. It is paid when the deed is offered for recording.

Who collects the documentary fee in Arapahoe County?

The Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder collects it when a deed or other instrument that conveys title is offered for recording.

How much would the fee be on a $500,000 sale?

About $50, applying the statutory rate of one cent per $100. Added liens or charges counted as consideration would raise the figure.

Is my deed treated as residential or commercial?

Residential by default. It is treated as non-residential only if the deed says so conspicuously when it is signed.

Do Aurora houses always record in Arapahoe County?

No. Aurora lies in Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties, and a deed is recorded in the county where the parcel is located.

Where can I get the current per-document recording fee?

Ask the Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder directly.

What does the Douglas County Clerk and Recorder's recording division do?

The Recording Division records, indexes, copies and preserves permanent public documents, primarily real estate records.

Under Colorado law that includes the deeds and mortgages behind every house sale in the county. The same office also issues marriage and civil union licenses, books first-time passport appointments and posts special district public notices.

When you sell a Douglas County house, the closing agent records the deed here, and the recorded document becomes part of the public chain of title that the next owner and lender will rely on.

Is there a way to watch for title fraud in Douglas County?

Yes. The Recording Division offers a free fraud detection service that alerts you any time a document is recorded in your name or on your property.

This service is aimed at "title theft," where someone records a false deed. It is worth signing up for if you own a vacant house, a rental or an inherited property that nobody visits often. Vacant properties are the ones where a bad filing can sit unnoticed for months.

Sign up before you list, and keep the alert on while a sale is pending so you see your own deed hit the record.

If an alert ever shows a filing you do not recognize, call the Clerk and Recorder's office and your title company right away. The office is open Monday through Friday during business hours, and a quick call is cheaper than untangling a bad deed after a sale falls through.

Where is the recording office, and who can use it?

The county offices are on Wilcox Street in Castle Rock, the county seat since 1874.

  • Street address for hand delivery: 301 Wilcox Street, Castle Rock, CO 80104
  • Mailing address: P.O. Box 1360, Castle Rock, CO 80104
  • Land records hours: Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  • Checks payable to Douglas County Clerk & Recorder

Electronic recording is offered to high-volume businesses through a county-approved third-party vendor, and it is not available to individuals. In a typical sale the title or escrow company sends the deed, so a seller rarely carries a document to the counter.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Douglas County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What does it cost to record a deed in Douglas County?

The county lists a recording fee of $43 per document for standard page sizes, plus a state documentary fee tied to the sale price.

ItemFee
Standard document (8.5 x 14 to 24 x 36)$43 per document
Land survey plat$50
UCC filing, 1 to 2 pages$13
UCC filing, 3 or more pages$18
Death certificates and DD-214Free
State documentary fee$0.01 per $100 if consideration is over $500

Technology surcharges are already included in the county's listed fees. The only sale-price charge on this listing is the documentary fee. Confirm current amounts with the office, because fees can change.

What does a deed need before it can be recorded in Douglas County?

The county publishes a checklist of requirements for documents submitted for recording, so read it before sending anything.

We did not verify each line of that checklist, so these are the general steps a seller can take:

  • Have the closing or title company prepare and submit the deed
  • Make sure the legal description matches your prior deed
  • Keep the recorded copy and its reception number for your files
  • Ask the office for a copy if you do not receive one

If a document is rejected, the delay can push back a closing date, and that is one reason a straightforward cash transaction with an experienced title company moves faster.

What is the history of the county that keeps these records?

Douglas County was created November 1, 1861 as one of the original 17 counties of the Colorado Territory and named for Senator Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois.

Its records have been kept in more than one place. The county seat started in Franktown, moved to California Ranch in 1863 and settled in Castle Rock in 1874. That year most of the eastern part of the county went to Elbert County.

The county covers about 843 square miles and had 357,978 residents in 2020.

What communities and employers shape home sales in Douglas County?

Highlands Ranch is the largest community, with Castle Rock, Parker, Lone Tree and Castle Pines also generating many recordings.

A 2015 employer report put the school district first at 5,563 workers, followed by Charles Schwab at 2,400 and EchoStar at 2,010. Douglas County School District RE-1 covers the county and is the third-largest district in Colorado.

Plum Creek and Cherry Creek flow north from the county, and three state parks lie within it: Castlewood Canyon, Chatfield and Roxborough. Land near creeks and open space is often described in recorded easements, which is another reason the recorded record matters.

Does recording a sale change what the Assessor does?

A change of ownership is one of the triggers for a Notice of Value, so a recorded sale can lead the Assessor to send the new owner a notice.

Douglas County says only properties with a change in value, use or ownership receive a notice, and that is fewer than 10% of owners. For 2026 the notices went out May 1, and written objections were due June 8.

  • Assessor's Office: 301 Wilcox Street, Castle Rock, 303-660-7450
  • County general information: 303-660-7400
  • Business personal property appeals ran June 15 through June 30, 2026

If you sell during appeal season, tell the buyer which valuation notices you received so they know what is pending.

What if taxes are unpaid when the deed is recorded?

Unpaid taxes can reach the tax lien sale, and the lien does not disappear because the deed changes hands.

The Treasurer says the buyer of a tax lien holds a lien, not the property, and that the interest rate is nine points above the federal discount rate as of September 1. The 2026 rate is 13%. Douglas County also states that eventual transfer of a deed occurs in less than 1 percent of purchases.

Ask your title company to run a tax check before the deed is signed, so any balance is paid from proceeds and the recorded deed is clean.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Which state programs might change a Douglas County seller's tax picture?

Colorado lists a property tax rebate, deferral, work-off program, senior exemption and veteran with a disability exemption.

Residential property is taxed at two state-set rates for 2026, 6.8% for local governments and 7.05% for schools. Revenue stays in the county and supports schools, counties, special districts, municipalities and junior colleges. Questions can go to the state Division of Property Taxation at (303) 864-7777.

How do taxes tie in to a Douglas County deed?

Property tax is separate from recording, but a sale usually settles both at closing.

The Treasurer runs the 2026 internet tax lien sale on November 5, 2026 at 13% interest. A clear recorded deed and paid taxes help a sale close without surprises.

Frequently asked questions

Who records deeds in Douglas County, Colorado?

The Douglas County Clerk and Recorder's Recording Division, in Castle Rock.

Is there free fraud protection for Douglas County property?

Yes. The Recording Division offers a free alert service that tells you when a document is recorded in your name or on your property.

What is the recording fee in Douglas County?

$43 per standard document, plus the state documentary fee of $0.01 per $100 of consideration over $500.

Can individuals e-record in Douglas County?

No. Electronic recording is offered to high-volume businesses through an approved vendor, so individuals use paper or a title company.

What are the land records hours?

Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., at 301 Wilcox Street, Castle Rock. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1360, Castle Rock, CO 80104, with checks payable to Douglas County Clerk & Recorder.

Does Douglas County record deeds for sales of inherited houses?

Yes. The Recording Division records the deeds and mortgages for real estate in the county, whatever the type of sale. A title company usually prepares and submits the paperwork for you.

Where is the Weld County Clerk and Recorder and when is it open?

The Weld County Clerk and Recorder is at 1250 H Street in Greeley, with a mailing address of PO Box 459, Greeley, CO 80632. The office phone is (970) 304-6530, and the email is crstaff@weld.gov.

Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The county's recording FAQ adds one detail that matters at a closing: documents accepted after 4:30 p.m. go on the next day's business, so a deed handed in late in the afternoon is not recorded that day.

What does it cost to record a deed in Weld County?

Weld County charges $43.00 to record a letter or legal size document, no matter how many pages it has. A state documentary fee applies on top of that when a document conveys real property for more than $500.

The county's fee schedule sets the documentary fee at $.01 per $100 of sale price. As an illustration, a $450,000 sale produces a documentary fee of $45.00, and a $300,000 sale produces $30.00. The schedule lists no separate county transfer tax.

ItemFee listed by Weld County
Letter or legal size document$43.00 regardless of pages
Maps and plats$43.00 regardless of pages
State documentary fee (C.R.S. 39-13-102)$.01 per $100 if the price is over $500
Real estate UCC, electronic$8.00
Real estate UCC, paper$13.00 for 1-2 pages, $18.00 for 3 or more
Death certificate recordingNo charge
Regular copies, in office or by mail$.25 per page
Certified copy$.25 per page plus $1.00 per document

Recording fees are set by statute, and the office returns documents that arrive with too little money. Checks should be payable to the Weld County Clerk and Recorder or to WCCR, and they need a signature.

What must a deed include before Weld County will accept it?

A deed needs a legible original, the right margins, a grantee mailing address and the correct fee. The county's recording page lists the requirements, and most rejections trace back to one of them.

  • Margins: at least one inch top and bottom and at least half an inch left and right (C.R.S. 30-10-406(3)(a)).
  • Grantee address: every deed must show the legal mailing address of the grantee (C.R.S. 38-35-109(2)), because the county uses it to mail future tax statements.
  • Legibility: poor originals make poor public records, and an illegible document is recorded as received with a clerk's note.
  • Return address: clearly mark where the recorded original should go.
  • Order: if you send several documents, send them in the order you want them recorded.
  • No personal data: do not place Social Security numbers or other personal information on a document, because recorded documents are public records.

The clerk does not give legal advice, does not prepare or notarize documents, and does not stock blank forms. Recording a document also does not confer legality or authenticity, so the deed itself should come from a title company or attorney.

Which county should record my deed?

The county where the land sits records the deed. Weld County's own page warns that documents sent to the wrong county are not rejected and the recording fees are not refunded, so the legal description and county should be checked before anything is mailed.

This is a live concern in Weld because several towns straddle county lines. Wikipedia marks Windsor, Johnstown, Erie, Berthoud, Lochbuie, Longmont, Brighton, Northglenn and Thornton as having portions in an adjacent county. A parcel in Windsor, for example, can fall in Weld or Larimer, and the recorder for that county takes the deed.

How do I find who owns a Weld County property or look up recorded documents?

Ownership lookups go through the County Assessor, and document searches go through Weld County's self-service website. The clerk's FAQ says the Assessor's site has a Property Information and Mapping section, and the Assessor's office is at 1400 N 17th Avenue in Greeley, phone (970) 353-3845.

Searching the document index online is free. Viewing and printing an image costs money, either by a monthly fee or per document. Online copies run $.50 for the first page and $.25 for each additional page, and certified online copies add $1.00 per document.

Who releases a deed of trust and who handles the tax bill?

Those are separate offices from the recorder. The Clerk's FAQ sends owners to the Weld County Public Trustee to release a deed of trust, and to the Weld County Treasurer for property tax questions. Both use the same building at 1400 N. 17th Avenue in Greeley and the phone number (970) 400-3290.

When a loan is paid off at a sale, the lender's release is handled through the Public Trustee, and the title company normally tracks that for you. Name changes on the tax roll follow the deed: the Treasurer states that a name change can only be done by a deed, and the Assessor updates the name after the deed is recorded with the Clerk and Recorder.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Weld County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What else does the Weld County recording office handle?

Beyond deeds, the recording department issues marriage and civil union licenses, accepts passport applications, and gives out military discharge copies. A marriage or civil union license costs $30.00, cash only, and appointments are required. Passport execution is $35.00 and the photo is $15.00, with State Department fees on top.

A DD 214 copy is free to the veteran or, if the veteran has died, to the veteran's parents, siblings, widow or widower and children, with photo identification. People who want their personal information blocked from public dissemination can use the office's request form.

What is Weld County like for someone selling a house here?

Weld County is large, fast-growing and mostly agricultural. Greeley is the county seat, and the county was organized on November 1, 1861, taking its name from Lewis Ledyard Weld, a territorial secretary. It covers 4,017 square miles, which makes it the third-largest county in Colorado by area.

The 2020 census counted 328,981 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 378,426. Weld as Colorado's leading producer of cattle, grain and sugar beets and an important oil and gas area in the Denver-Julesburg Basin. Interstates 25 and 76 serve the county, along with US 34, US 85 and State Highway 14.

Seventeen school districts serve the county, among them Greeley District 6, Windsor RE-4, Thompson R-2J and St. Vrain Valley RE 1J. A seller in one of the smaller eastern towns and a seller in a Front Range suburb face quite different buyer pools, but they all record at the same Greeley office.

How does a cash sale fit into this process?

A cash sale uses the same recording steps. The seller signs a deed, the title company confirms the legal description and grantee address, pays the recording and documentary fees, and the clerk records the deed. Without a buyer's lender, there is no loan underwriting or appraisal to wait on, which is why cash closings can be scheduled quickly once title is clear.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Weld County, Colorado?

It costs $43.00 for a letter or legal size document regardless of page count, plus the state documentary fee of $.01 per $100 of sale price when the price is over $500.

What is the Weld County Clerk and Recorder's address?

The office is at 1250 H Street in Greeley, Colorado, with a mailing address of PO Box 459, Greeley, CO 80632, and the phone number is (970) 304-6530.

Does Weld County charge a transfer tax?

The county's recording fee schedule lists the state documentary fee and no separate county transfer tax. The documentary fee is $.01 per $100 of price on documents conveying real property for more than $500.

What happens if I record a deed in the wrong county?

Weld County does not reject documents meant for another county and does not refund recording fees, so confirm the county and legal description first.

What does a Colorado deed need to show about the buyer?

It must show the legal mailing address of the grantee, as required by C.R.S. 38-35-109(2), so tax statements can be mailed to the new owner.

Can the Weld County clerk help me prepare my deed?

No. Clerks cannot give legal advice, prepare or notarize documents, so use a title company or attorney for the deed itself.

Who records deeds in Boulder County?

The Boulder County Clerk and Recorder records deeds, deeds of trust, liens, plats and court documents for every property in the county. Its Recording Division is at 1750 33rd St., Suite 201, in Boulder, and you can reach it at 303-413-7770 or recording@bouldercounty.gov.

Recording is what makes a sale part of the public record. When a house changes hands, the signed deed goes to this office, and the buyer's lender records its deed of trust at the same time.

How big is Boulder County, and which towns does the recorder serve?

Boulder County covers about 740 square miles, with 726 of them land, and its seat is the City of Boulder. The Territory of Colorado created it on November 1, 1861 as one of the original 17 counties.

The incorporated places are listed below. Longmont and Erie reach into Weld County, and Superior reaches into Jefferson County, so a deed for a house near those lines still goes to the county where the parcel sits.

  • Boulder, Lafayette, Longmont, Louisville, Erie
  • Jamestown, Lyons, Nederland, Superior, Ward
  • Unincorporated communities include Niwot, Gunbarrel, Gold Hill, Eldora and Allenspark

Rocky Mountain National Park lies partly in the county, and Longs Peak, at 14,255 feet, is inside its borders. In 2001 a 27.5 square mile corner of the county became part of the City and County of Broomfield, so older records for that area sit here.

What does it cost to record a deed in Boulder County?

Recording a document costs $43, a fee that took effect July 1, 2025, plus the state documentary fee when it applies. The county lists these charges.

ItemFee
Recording fee, per document$43
Documentary fee$0.01 per $100 of consideration, on non-exempt deeds over $500
Certifying a copy of a recorded document$1
Non-digital copies$0.25 per page
UCC recording, 1 to 2 pages$13
UCC recording, 3 or more pages$18
E-recorded UCC$8
Recording a death certificateNo charge

The county page lists no per-page recording fee. Questions about fees it does not list go to the office phone number above. Checks are payable to Boulder County Clerk & Recorder.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Boulder County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How does the documentary fee work on a sale?

The documentary fee is a state charge of one cent for each $100 of consideration once the price passes $500. It is set by C.R.S. 39-13-102 and collected by the county clerk and recorder.

The statute counts the price plus any lien or encumbrance and the charges paid to make the transfer. On a $600,000 house that works out to $600. The same statute treats a property as residential unless the deed carries a conspicuous note that it is not.

The county fee page lists the documentary fee as the only charge tied to the price of a deed. Treasurer's, public trustee's and sheriff's deeds are exempt under Broomfield's published fee schedule, which tracks the same statute.

How can you submit a document to the Boulder County recorder?

You can mail it, drop it in a 24-hour box, bring it in, or have a title company e-record it. Each route has its own limits.

  • Mail: send it to the Recording Division with the document, a check and a return address.
  • Drop boxes: 1750 33rd St. in Boulder, 1755 S. Public Road in Lafayette, and 529 Coffman St. in Longmont. Mark the folder "Recording" and add contact details.
  • In person: Monday through Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. The office is closed Fridays.
  • Email: individual owners can send a scanned PDF, with extra fees, but not brokerages, title companies, lenders or law firms.
  • E-recording: high-volume filers use Simplifile, eRecording Partners, CSC or Indecomm. This is the only option described as same-day.

Drop-offs in Lafayette or Longmont go by interoffice mail to Boulder, which can add one to two business days.

What should a deed include before it is recorded?

A deed needs the right fee, a return address, and no personal identifying information, because recorded documents are public. Boulder County's page asks you to remove such details before filing.

Recorded documents cannot be pulled back by the clerk, and the staff cannot advise on which document to file. For a house sale, a title company or attorney drafts the deed and checks the legal description. A cash buyer works the same way, and the closing agent handles the recording step.

The county runs a public search site where you can find recorded documents, download free copies and order certified ones. It is the quickest way to confirm a deed or lien before you list.

What do Census figures show for Boulder County housing?

The Census Bureau counts 328,560 residents in Boulder County as of July 1, 2025, compared with 330,758 in the 2020 count. These are the QuickFacts figures for 2020 through 2024.

MeasureBoulder County
Owner-occupied housing rate62.0%
Median value, owner-occupied homes$756,300
Median gross rent$1,966
Households137,008
Persons per household2.30
Median household income$103,994
Land area726.38 square miles

Outside the city of Boulder, the county's owner share is higher than the city's, so a typical seller here is more often a homeowner than a landlord.

How have fires and floods affected recording and property here?

Two disasters in the past decade left a mark on Boulder County property records. The Marshall Fire of December 30, 2021 destroyed an estimated 1,084 structures and damaged 149 more across 6,026 acres, with evacuations in Superior, Louisville and unincorporated Boulder County.

Wind gusts reached 115 mph, and the damage exceeded $2 billion. The sheriff's 2023 finding gave two causes: embers on Twelve Tribes property and a sparking Xcel Energy power line.

The September 2013 floods destroyed 262 county homes and damaged nearly 300. A deed for a fire-damaged lot is recorded the same way as any other, and the same fee table applies.

What do sellers in Boulder County usually face?

Sellers here deal with high values, mixed ownership and mountain weather. A few points come up again and again.

  • Estates and inherited houses, where court documents such as letters may need recording.
  • Rentals with tenants and licensing steps that change when ownership changes.
  • Back property tax, which the title company pays out of proceeds.
  • Houses in areas hit by the 2013 floods or the 2021 fire, where the history is part of the buyer's questions.

Court documents such as letters and personal representative deeds are among the items the recorder accepts, so an estate sale can be recorded in the same office. Other accepted items include warranty deeds, quit claim deeds, plats and military records.

The Treasurer also takes payments in Longmont on Mondays and in Boulder on weekdays, but the recorder's counter is a separate office from the Treasurer, so confirm which one you need before you drive over. A tax payoff goes to the Treasurer at 303-441-3520, and a deed goes to the Clerk and Recorder at 303-413-7770.

If you are selling a house that sits in more than one county, the statute splits the documentary fee between the county recorders in the same ratio as the value in each county, with the person recording the deed making the allocation.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Boulder County?

The recording fee is $43 per document as of July 1, 2025. If the price is over $500, add the state documentary fee of one cent per $100 of consideration.

Is the Boulder County recorder open on Fridays?

No. The office is open Monday through Thursday from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and is closed Fridays. The three 24-hour drop boxes stay available.

Does Colorado charge a transfer tax on a house sale?

The county fee page lists a documentary fee on deeds, and no separate transfer tax. It is one cent per $100 of consideration over $500, collected when the deed is recorded.

Can I e-record my own deed in Boulder County?

Individual owners can email a scanned PDF for a fee. E-recording through Simplifile, eRecording Partners, CSC or Indecomm is meant for high-volume filers such as title companies.

Where can I find an old Boulder County deed?

Use the county's public search site to find recorded documents, download free copies and order certified copies for $1. For land that moved to Broomfield in 2001, older records may sit in Boulder County.

Who records deeds in Denver County?

The Denver Clerk and Recorder's Recording Division records deeds and deeds of trust for Denver County. Because Denver is a consolidated city and county, the same city government also holds the Public Trustee, which runs foreclosures and releases of deeds of trust.

The Recording Division is at 200 W. 14th Ave., Denver, CO 80204. Most services are available remotely, and in-person visits need an appointment. The Record Documents page says arriving more than ten minutes late may mean rescheduling.

Denver County is bordered by Adams, Arapahoe and Jefferson counties, and a deed for a house inside Denver's boundaries goes here, not to a neighboring county.

What does recording a document cost in Denver?

A standard document costs $43. The table lists the charges on the Denver recording page.

ItemCharge
Standard document$43 per document
Certified copy$1 certification plus $0.25 per page

The recording division notes elsewhere on its main page that fees are rising on July 1 to comply with a new state law, without listing the new amounts. Confirm the current figure before you send a check.

Does Denver charge a transfer tax on a house sale?

The Denver pages we opened list a documentary fee of $0.10 per $1,000 on real estate grants and conveyances, and they list no separate city transfer tax.

On a $500,000 sale, that fee works out to $50. The page says no fee applies to amounts under $500.

How do you submit a deed for recording in Denver?

E-recording is the recommended route, and Denver says mailed documents can take 7 to 10 days while e-recording takes minutes.

  • E-recording vendors named on the page: EPN and CSC.
  • By mail: send the document, a self-addressed envelope and a check or money order payable to Manager of Finance.
  • In person: cash, check, money order or credit card (Mastercard, Visa, Discover). Temporary checks are not accepted.
  • By phone: Denver cannot take card information over the phone.

Most sellers never do this themselves, because the title or escrow company handles the recording of a deed at closing.

What formatting rules apply to Denver documents?

Documents need a one-inch top margin and half-inch side margins, citing C.R.S. 30-10-406(3)(a). The largest paper size is 24 by 36 inches.

Surveys have to be on paper, and a non-paper survey adds a $5 per page paper copy fee. Liens must be notarized before submission. Staff cannot give legal advice or help fill out forms.

One rule catches people out. The page states that Denver County cannot reject or refund a document recorded in the wrong county, so the person submitting it has to choose the right county.

How are deeds of trust released in Denver?

The Public Trustee processes a release when a loan is paid off or refinanced. The lender or title company files it, and the recorded release shows up in Denver's recorded document search.

Three items go in: a signed and notarized Release of Deed of Trust, the deed of trust, and the original promissory note marked paid or cancelled. The page recommends filing electronically through Simplifile or Corporation Service Company, and mailing by certified mail if you cannot.

For a seller, an old loan that was paid off years ago but never released can slow a closing. Ask the title company to search for unreleased deeds of trust early.

What is the satisfaction of judgment process in Denver?

Clearing a recorded judgment takes steps in two offices. The Denver recording page lays them out.

  1. Mail the Acknowledgment of Satisfaction to the Denver District Court Clerk at 1437 Bannock St., Room 256, with a $20 certificate fee by cashier's check or money order and a stamped return envelope.
  2. Send the certificate to the Clerk and Recorder with the $43 recording fee and a self-addressed envelope.
  3. Send copies of the recorded certificate to the three credit bureaus, because the Recorder does not report to them.

A judgment lien that stays on record against a house can show up in a title search at closing.

What should a Denver seller expect from the recording step?

At closing, the title company records the deed, any release of the old deed of trust and the new buyer's documents. Denver's online recorded document database is where those documents then appear.

Records that sometimes cause delay include an unreleased deed of trust, a recorded judgment, a tax lien and, for inherited houses, a beneficiary deed or proof of death. Fixing these before listing, or before accepting an offer, keeps the closing date from slipping.

If you want a written cash offer on a Denver County house with title problems, an unreleased loan or a tax balance, call us and we will look at it as is.

What else does the Denver Recording Division handle?

Beyond deeds, the division also issues marriage licenses and records civil unions, and it takes campaign finance reports for the city. The division page says marriage and recording services both require an appointment, and it urges people not to wait until the last minute.

The Public Trustee unit holds property titles in trust when a property secures a loan. Its two main jobs are running foreclosures, including auction sales when needed, and executing releases of deeds of trust to remove mortgage liens. The page has a resource section for homeowners whose house sold at auction.

You can search land, marriage and other public records through the division's site. For general city questions the page lists 3-1-1, or (720) 913-1311 from outside Denver.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Where does a Colorado beneficiary deed get recorded for a Denver house?

It is recorded here, with the Denver Clerk and Recorder, and it has to be recorded before the owner dies. Colorado's beneficiary deed statute requires recording in the county where the property is located, and the sample form warns in capitals that an unrecorded deed does not work (C.R.S. 15-15-404).

The standard $43 recording fee applies to that document on the Denver fee list. A revocation of a beneficiary deed is also recorded with the clerk and recorder in the property's county under 15-15-405.

When a Denver owner has died and a buyer wants to purchase, the title company searches this same record for any beneficiary deed, later revocation or other recorded claim.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Denver County Clerk and Recorder?

The Recording Division is at 200 W. 14th Ave., Denver, CO 80204. In-person service needs an appointment, and mail or electronic submission is also available.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Denver?

The listed charge is $43 per document, plus the documentary fee of $0.10 per $1,000 on conveyances where it applies. Confirm the current amount, since the office has announced fee changes tied to a new state law.

Can I e-record a deed in Denver?

Yes. The county recommends it and names EPN and CSC as approved vendors. It says e-recording takes minutes against 7 to 10 days for mail.

What is the fee for releasing a deed of trust in Denver?

$73 total, which includes the $43 recording fee and a $30 Public Trustee execution fee.

Who do checks go to for Denver recording?

Checks and money orders are payable to Manager of Finance. Temporary checks are not accepted in person.

What happens if I record a deed in the wrong county?

Denver County cannot reject or refund a document recorded in the wrong county, so the person submitting it must pick the correct one.

What does the El Paso County Clerk and Recorder do when a house is sold?

The El Paso County Clerk and Recorder records the deed that moves a house from the seller to the buyer, and it records the deed of trust and the release that go with a mortgage. The office also collects the state documentary fee on the sale at the moment the deed is filed.

Recording is what puts the sale in the public record. Until a deed is recorded, the county records still show the old owner. Most sellers never visit the office, because the title or settlement company handles the filing after closing. It still helps to know what the office charges and why a filing can bounce back.

The recording department takes questions at (719) 520-6200 or by email at recweb@elpasoco.com, according to the county fee page.

What does it cost to record a deed in El Paso County?

Since July 1, 2025, El Paso County charges a flat $43 to record a standard document, no matter how many pages it has. On a deed that transfers title for more than $500, the state documentary fee is added at one cent for every $100 of the price.

The county explained that the $43 is a $40 state-set flat fee plus a $1 Electronic Recording Technology Board surcharge and a $2 electronic filing surcharge. The change follows House Bill 24-1269. For a sale at $400,000, the documentary fee works out to $40, so recording the deed alone would be $83 under these rules (an illustration, not a quote).

How do I get a deed to the El Paso County recorder?

There are three routes: the drop box, the mail, or eRecording through the county's online process. A seller selling to a cash buyer usually leaves this to the closing company.

  • Drop box: outside the east entrance of the main office at the Citizens Service Center, 1675 W. Garden of the Gods Road. Seal the envelope, enclose payment, and add a phone number.
  • Mail: El Paso County Clerk & Recorder, Attn: Recording, P.O. Box 2007, Colorado Springs, CO 80901-2007. The return address belongs on the front of the document.
  • eRecording: the county points customers to its eRecording software page for online submission.

To get a copy of a recorded document, email copyrequests@elpasoco.com. The office says it answers copy requests within 48 hours. Documents recorded before 1996 are held only at the Citizens Service Center.

Why do deeds get rejected in El Paso County?

Most rejections come from small errors the county lists in its recording checklist, and a rejected deed delays the date the buyer shows up in the public record.

  • Wrong fee. Recording fees are set by statute, and the county can reject a filing with the wrong amount or a wrong page count.
  • Missing documentary fee. Any exemption has to be claimed on the face of the document, or the fee is due. The consideration figure must match on the deed and the transfer declaration.
  • No grantee address. Colorado law (C.R.S. 38-35-109(2)) requires the buyer's mailing address on the deed, because it decides where future tax statements are sent.
  • Margins. C.R.S. 30-10-406(3)(a) calls for a one inch top margin and half inch left, right and bottom margins.
  • Check problems. Checks go to the El Paso County Clerk, must be signed, and must not be stale dated. A bad check sends back every document stapled to it.
  • Faint notary seals. An embossed seal that is not inked will not show on the scanned image.

What does the clerk not do, and who handles those steps?

The recorder does not search titles or fix ownership questions. Under C.R.S. 30-10-101(2.5c), the office is not required to search the real estate records to find a document for copying or any other purpose.

  • Releases of deed of trust go through the El Paso County Public Trustee first, at 1675 West Garden of the Gods Road, Suite 2100, before they are recorded.
  • Property tax status certificates come from the County Treasurer. A Certificate of Taxes Due costs $10.
  • If a recorded change of title does not show up in the assessment records after several weeks, the office tells owners to call the County Assessor at (719) 520-6600.
  • A title company can supply an Ownership and Encumbrances report showing the current owner and any open liens.
  • Wills, probate and small estate forms are handled by the Fourth Judicial District Court at 270 S. Tejon St.

Inherited houses are common in this county. If a parent's name is still on the deed, updating it is a separate recording, and the clerk's own advice is to use a title company or attorney for the right instrument.

How can El Paso County owners protect against deed fraud?

The clerk suggests checking the county records at least once a year for deeds or mortgages you did not sign. This matters most for vacant houses, rentals run from out of town, and properties in an estate.

  • Search the recording website, www.epcrecords.com, once a year.
  • Make sure the Assessor has the right mailing address for you.
  • Call the Assessor and Treasurer if tax bills stop arriving.
  • Check a vacant property often, or ask someone you trust to do it.
  • Update the deed when a family member dies and someone else inherits.

What is El Paso County like for a home seller?

El Paso County is the most populous county in Colorado, with 730,395 residents in the 2020 Census, and its seat is Colorado Springs. It covers 2,130 square miles, borders Pueblo, Fremont, Teller, Douglas, Elbert, Lincoln and Crowley counties, and became one of the original 17 Colorado counties on November 1, 1861.

Six incorporated municipalities: Colorado Springs, Fountain, Manitou Springs, Monument, Palmer Lake and Calhan. Unincorporated communities include Falcon, Eastonville, Ramah and Yoder, so a rural or edge-of-county home can sit outside any city.

The military is the largest employer group. A 2022 report listed Fort Carson at 36,000 employees, Peterson Space Force Base at 10,650, Schriever Space Force Base at 8,000 and the U.S. Air Force Academy at 7,650.

Frequently asked questions

How much does El Paso County charge to record a deed?

The county charges a flat $43 per document since July 1, 2025, plus a documentary fee of one cent per $100 of price on deeds over $500. Release of deed of trust documents go through the Public Trustee first.

Can I e-record a deed in El Paso County as an individual?

The county's recording page says customers can record through eRecording software and links to details. For a single deed, the drop box, the mail, or your closing company are the simplest routes.

How long does it take to get a copy of a recorded deed?

The county states it responds to emailed copy requests within 48 hours. Copies are $0.25 per page, and a certified copy costs $1 more per document.

Who pays the documentary fee on a house sale?

Colorado law puts the fee on whoever offers the deed for recording. Who covers it in a given sale depends on the purchase contract, so check the contract and ask your closing company.

Where is the El Paso County recording office?

The main office is in the Citizens Service Center at 1675 W. Garden of the Gods Road, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Union Town Center branch at 8830 N. Union Blvd. also takes recordings on Saturdays from 8:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.

What if a lien is still on my title after I sold?

A release has to be recorded by the lien holder. For a mortgage, the lender files a Release of Deed of Trust through the Public Trustee, and the recorder then records it. You can email copyrequests@elpasoco.com for a copy.
